tagline: Lake views and mountain estates along roads linking Winnipesaukee’s shore towns
intro: The Lakes Region Tour circles Lake Winnipesaukee, with NH 11 following the shore between Alton and Gilford. New Hampshire’s tourism division promotes this scenic byway for lake and mountain scenery, including views across the water toward the Ossipee Range. The drive links Weirs Beach’s arcades with the shore towns and the eastern side, which the tourism division describes as less developed.

One part of this road network began with a provincial order in 1722 to build a road from Dover to the Lakes Region west of Winnipesaukee. Alton’s Main Street follows that route. An eighteenth-century road to Wolfeboro met it at an acute angle, shaping the junction that became Alton’s town center. Rail service later brought a rerouting of the Wolfeboro road. The junction’s angled layout remains in Monument Square, where most of the surrounding buildings face the triangular space. Alton chose the old Wolfeboro Road alignment for its town hall in 1893, after the road had moved.

For a circuit beginning at Weirs Beach, head toward Gilford and follow NH 11 along the shore to Alton Bay and Alton. NH 28 continues north to Wolfeboro; NH 109 leads through Melvin Village toward Moultonborough, the town containing Castle in the Clouds. Continue through Center Harbor to Meredith on NH 25, then return south to Weirs Beach on US 3.

moments.title: Endicott Rock
moments.text: A colonial boundary survey left its lettering on a rock at Weirs Beach in 1652. The Massachusetts Bay Colony’s charter placed its boundary three miles north of the Merrimack River. The English surveyors incorrectly took this location for the river’s northernmost head. The rock was originally in the lake. The Merrimack’s main tributary, the Pemigewasset River, has headwaters significantly farther north than the spot marked by the surveyors. Their inscriptions include Governor John Endecott’s name and their own initials. After nineteenth-century dredging rediscovered the rock, the state built a protective pavilion and stabilized cracks with iron fittings.
moments.notice: The rock’s carved lettering includes the governor’s name and the surveyors’ initials.

moments.title: Wolfeboro
moments.text: Wolfeboro’s summer-estate history belongs to Lake Wentworth as well as Winnipesaukee. Colonial Governor John Wentworth established Kingswood beside Lake Wentworth in 1771. The town later became a summer colony for families from Boston and southern New Hampshire. Its motto calls it “The Oldest Summer Resort in America.” The main village sits at the head of Wolfeboro Bay, where routes 28 and 109 meet. The Smith River carries Lake Wentworth’s outflow into Winnipesaukee. Wolfeboro Falls lies one mile north of the main village along routes 28 and 109; Lake Wentworth also has its own state park on the shore.

moments.title: Castle in the Clouds
moments.text: Shoe manufacturer Thomas Gustave Plant’s mountain house combined Craftsman design with a circular shower and central vacuum system. Built in 1913–1914 for his second wife, Olive Cornelia Dewey, the sixteen-room mansion stands on a rocky outcrop of Lee Mountain above Lake Winnipesaukee. Architect J. Williams Beal designed it with help from his sons. Plant lost his money in the 1930s, but creditors allowed him to remain until his death in 1941. Richard and Donald Robie bought the estate in 1956 and opened it as a tourist attraction. The estate is now owned and operated by the nonprofit Castle Preservation Society.
moments.notice: The house overlooks Lake Winnipesaukee and the Ossipee Mountains from Lee Mountain’s rocky outcrop.
